after.text:
The remaining parts of this article are organized as follows. The next two sec-
tions contain the proofs of Theorem 1 and Theorem 2. For the sake of completeness
we give the proofs of the corollaries in the fourth section. In the last but one sec-
tion we discuss the special case φ = 0 and how our results provide new information
about Gram points. Finally, we conclude with some remarks on the shape of the
curve t 7→ ζ( 21 + it) and further applications of our method.

section_entries.mathematical_role: Defines the phase/intersection representation, counting functions, main counting and moment theorems, directional corollaries, and an equidistribution obstruction.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Directional means and arbitrarily large values on half-lines
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Translates the counting and moment laws into conditional directional means, an unconditional zero mean on the imaginary axis, positivity of real components, and unconditional arbitrarily large values on prescribed right-half-plane half-lines.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Monotone phase rotation converts root counts to a winding number
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Uses the logarithmic derivative asymptotic to show that Δ rotates monotonically with increasing speed, identifies roots of a prescribed phase with a winding number, integrates the rotation rate, and removes a convenient endpoint assumption with a controlled error.

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: The result isolates genuine nonzero crossings by excluding phase roots that are also zeta zeros. Its directional lower bound collapses exactly at the imaginary axis, exposing a real obstruction rather than a missing cosmetic case.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: Corollary 5 gives a linear-in-T lower bound for roots of the prescribed Δ-phase equation with ζ(1/2+it) nonzero when φ≠π/2. No nontrivial bound is obtained for φ=π/2. The authors point to Fujii's conjectured equidistribution of Δ-phases at zeta-zero ordinates as a possible source of further information.
directed.conceptual_reading: The exclusion ζ≠0 separates geometric crossings from zeros at the origin. The exceptional direction records degeneration of the available moment-based control, while the proposed equidistribution would control overlap between two discrete phase sets.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The counted set is the bridge: prescribed Δ-phase roots minus coincident zeta zeros represents nonzero intersections of the zeta curve with a line. Fujii's phase sequence would provide a distributional way to estimate the removed overlap.
directed.boundary_or_failure: The source explicitly supplies no imaginary-axis lower bound, and the equidistribution input is conjectural. The figure is illustrative only. This span does not show that the exceptional count is small or finite.
directed.uncertainty: The extracted numerical constant and exponent spacing in the lower bound are formula-fragile; only the positive linear bound away from φ=π/2 is safe without the scan.

supported: The span states a positive linear-in-T lower bound for nonzero prescribed-phase roots when φ is not π/2 and explicitly states that no nontrivial lower bound is available at φ=π/2.
It presents Fujii's equidistribution statement as conjectural and says that a proof would yield more information about the exceptional quantity.
The candidate correctly treats the figure as illustrative and does not claim an imaginary-axis count.
inference: Interpreting the ζ≠0 restriction as removal of phase roots coincident with zeta zeros is supported by the counted set.
Equidistribution of Δ-phases at zero ordinates could plausibly inform the size of the removed overlap, but the span does not derive an overlap estimate.
unsupported_or_imported: The claim that the exceptional direction records degeneration of 'moment-based control' imports a proof mechanism not present in this frozen span.
The candidate presents the equidistribution conjecture as a distributional method to estimate overlap more specifically than the source's statement that it would yield 'more information'.
context_or_ocr_risk: The displayed lower-bound constant and exponent layout are text-layer damaged; only positivity and linear T-scale away from π/2 are safe here.
missed_mechanism: The source does not identify why the available bound degenerates, so mechanism-level attribution must remain explicitly inferential.
revision_instructions: Remove the unsupported attribution to moment-based degeneration.
Recast the overlap discussion as a plausible inference from Fujii's conjecture, not as a result supplied by the span; retain the explicit no-bound and conjectural qualifications.

unit_result_entry.why_material: Relates the squared first moment to the product of the nonzero-sample count and second moment, yielding the lower bound for genuine line crossings after inserting the two moment asymptotics.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Second-moment mass forces a large value in every dyadic interval
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Compares the number of phase samples in (T,2T] with their second-moment mass to rule out a uniform sub-square-root-log bound, then uses the signed first moment to force the desired half-line sign; the exceptional imaginary direction uses its zero-mean relation to obtain both signs.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Gram points recast real-axis intersections and expose failures of sign alternation
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Specializes the phase roots to Gram points, introduces the real Hardy Z-function, relates sign changes to critical-line zeros, and interprets failures of Gram's law as negative real-axis intersections whose unbounded magnitude remains open.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: The sample count normalizes a first moment into a directional mean, the second moment forces large samples, and the signed first moment or a zero-mean symmetry is separately needed to place those samples on a desired half-line.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: General directional normalization is conditional on RH or almost-all critical-line zeros, while the imaginary-axis branch has a distinct unconditional argument.
related_synthesis_entries.title: Moments become geometric information only after the correct count and sign controls

section_entries.label: Concluding remarks
section_entries.mathematical_role: Synthesizes geometric meaning, averages directional means, proposes a small/large-value split, and identifies the extension boundary for other L-functions.

unit_result_entry.title: The method extends to Dirichlet L-functions but encounters higher-degree factorization barriers
unit_result_entry.why_material: Records that the mechanism transfers easily to Dirichlet L-functions but becomes difficult for higher-degree L-functions, with quadratic Dedekind zeta treated only by exploiting the factorization ζK=ζL and zero symmetry.

unit_dependency_entry.context_note: This is a scope/obstruction statement rather than a proved universal impossibility.
unit_dependency_entry.representation_dependency: Depends on the availability of a suitable factorization and compatible functional-equation symmetry.

neighboring_unit_entries.title: Averaging directional means suggests a small-versus-large intersection split
neighboring_unit_entries.why_material: Integrates the conditional means e^{iφ}cosφ over direction to obtain 1/2, relates that value to a separate a-point derivative phenomenon, and proposes the heuristic that each directional intersection set divides roughly equally between very small and large magnitudes around its mean.

related_synthesis_entries.claim: The proof depends not merely on a functional equation but on phase-factor expansions and Dirichlet-series kernels whose main terms remain tractable; factorization supplies that tractability in the cited quadratic Dedekind case.
related_synthesis_entries.limit: The paper states difficulty for higher degree and one successful factored case, not a necessary-and-sufficient transfer criterion.
related_synthesis_entries.title: The contour method's portability is governed by structural factorization

spontaneous.spontaneous_reading: Portability depends on structural factorization, not merely on possessing a functional equation. Dirichlet L-functions remain tractable, while higher-degree cases can lose the product structure that makes the contour kernels analyzable.

directed.source_grounded_mathematics: The authors state that their results extend easily to Dirichlet L-functions but that higher-degree L-functions are difficult. As evidence, they cite the quadratic Dedekind case, where ζ_K factors as ζL and a result on simple zeros uses that factorization together with symmetry of zeta zeros.
directed.conceptual_reading: Factorization decomposes a higher-degree object into familiar analytic components with compatible symmetries. It identifies a plausible transfer criterion: not degree alone, but whether the resulting phase and Dirichlet-series kernels remain tractable.
directed.representation_or_bridge: The bridge object is the factorization ζ_K=ζL, which exposes separate zeta and Dirichlet-L structures rather than treating ζ_K as an opaque higher-degree function.
directed.boundary_or_failure: This is a scope and obstruction statement, not a proof that every higher-degree extension is impossible or that factorization is necessary and sufficient. The cited simple-zero result is not itself the directional moment theorem.
directed.uncertainty: The qualitative extension boundary is explicit, but the span gives no detailed transferred formulas or complete criterion for higher-degree L-functions.

supported: The authors state that their results extend easily to Dirichlet L-functions and that higher-degree L-functions are difficult to handle.
They cite a quadratic Dedekind zeta example in which ζ_K=ζL factorization and symmetry of zeta zeros were used to prove infinitely many simple zeros.
The candidate correctly notes that the cited simple-zero result is not itself the directional moment theorem.
inference: Factorization is a plausible source of tractability in the cited quadratic example.
Compatible phase or Dirichlet-series kernels may matter for extending the present contour method, but this criterion is not developed in the span.
unsupported_or_imported: The spontaneous claim that portability 'depends on structural factorization' promotes one cited successful example into a general dependency not established by the source.
The claim that higher-degree cases lose the product structure that makes these contour kernels analyzable imports mechanism from other spans and is not stated here.
The proposed criterion based on tractable phase and Dirichlet-series kernels is reasonable research inference, not source-grounded mathematics from this unit.
paraphrase_or_style_risk: The strong portability slogan risks turning a narrow concluding remark into a generic transfer principle.
context_or_ocr_risk: The factorization ζ_K=ζL and qualitative scope statement are readable; no formula-level reconstruction is required.
missed_mechanism: The span supplies an example and a difficulty report, not evidence that factorization is necessary, sufficient, or the controlling obstruction for all higher-degree extensions.
revision_instructions: Rewrite the opening to say that factorization is the mechanism used in the cited quadratic Dedekind simple-zero result, not that general portability depends on it.
Keep the Dirichlet-versus-higher-degree scope statement and the distinction from the directional moment theorem.
Label any kernel-tractability criterion explicitly as a hypothesis suggested by the example rather than a conclusion of the span.
